concept.name: MySQL Replication Topologies

relationships.description: Connects MySQL Replication Topologies to database indexing in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: MySQL replication copies binary log (binlog) events from a primary server to one or more replicas to scale reads, isolate analytics, and survive node or availability-zone failures. Choosing between asynchronous, semi-synchronous, and Group Replication (Paxos-based) topologies trades write latency and operational complexity against Recovery Point Objective (RPO).
spark.keyTakeaway: Default to GTID-based asynchronous primary-replica with semi-synchronous replication (`rpl_semi_sync_master_wait_for_slave_count=1`) when you need zero data loss on single-node failure without paying full InnoDB Group Replication consensus latency.

concept.whyItMatters: A single MySQL primary hits CPU, IOPS, or connection limits quickly under read-heavy workloads and represents a single point of failure. Replication decouples read scaling and backup execution from the write path while providing warm standbys for sub-minute failover using Orchestrator or ProxySQL.
whenToUse: Read-to-write ratios exceed 5:1 and SELECT traffic (dashboards, search, reporting) saturates primary buffer pool or CPU.
You require zero-downtime schema changes (gh-ost or pt-online-schema-change), logical backups (mysqldump), or physical snapshots without stalling primary transactions.
High availability requires automatic promotion of an up-to-date standby within 10–30 seconds across availability zones.
whenNotToUse: Write throughput on a single table exceeds what one primary can commit (~15k–30k writes/sec depending on fsync and NVMe IOPS), because replicas must replay every write.
Applications require strict linearizable reads immediately after writes without session-stickiness, GTID wait (`WAIT_FOR_EXECUTED_GTID_SET`), or read-after-write routing.
Multi-region active-active writes on the same rows are required without conflict resolution; multi-primary Group Replication suffers certification conflicts and rollback spikes.
keyPoints: Enable Global Transaction Identifiers (`gtid_mode=ON`, `enforce_gtid_consistency=ON`) so replicas track committed transactions by UUID:sequence rather than fragile binlog file/position offsets.
Use `binlog_format=ROW` (`binlog_row_image=MINIMAL` or `FULL`) instead of `STATEMENT` to eliminate non-deterministic replay bugs from `UUID()`, `NOW()`, or `LIMIT` without `ORDER BY`.

Semi-synchronous replication (`AFTER_SYNC`) guarantees at least one replica has persisted the event to its relay log before the primary commits to InnoDB, preventing phantom reads and lost commits on crash.

Parallel replica appliers (`replica_parallel_type=LOGICAL_CLOCK`, `replica_parallel_workers=8`–`16`) apply non-conflicting transactions concurrently using commit-parent timestamps to curb replication lag.
InnoDB Group Replication (MySQL 8.0+) uses a Paxos variant (XCom) for certified multi-node consensus, ideal for single-primary HA clusters of 3 or 5 nodes with automatic split-brain protection.

examples.title: Zero-RPO Checkout Ledger with Semi-Sync Primary-Replica
examples.scenario: A fintech payments service processes 4,000 TPS on MySQL 8.0 across two AWS Availability Zones. Asynchronous replication risked losing up to 500ms of committed ledger entries during an abrupt primary EBS failure.
examples.outcome: Enabling `rpl_semi_sync_source_wait_point=AFTER_SYNC` with `AFTER_SYNC` acknowledgment to a same-region standby added only 0.8ms p99 write latency while guaranteeing RPO=0 on single-AZ loss, with automatic fallback to async after a 1,000ms timeout.

examples.title: Isolating Heavy BI Queries via Cascading Delayed Replica
examples.scenario: Analysts running 20-minute `GROUP BY` queries on a production read replica caused InnoDB history list length (HLL) to exceed 2 million and stalled purge threads, degrading replica apply speed.
examples.outcome: Deploying a dedicated intermediate relay replica feeding an analytics replica (plus a 4-hour `CHANGE REPLICATION SOURCE TO SOURCE_DELAY = 14400` DR node) isolated primary binlog dump threads and gave ops a 4-hour window to recover from accidental `DROP TABLE`.

tradeOffs.pro: Asynchronous replication returns commit success immediately after local binlog/InnoDB flush (~0.3ms), keeping primary p99 latency independent of network RTT.
tradeOffs.con: Committed transactions not yet shipped to replicas are permanently lost if the primary storage fails unrecoverably (RPO > 0).

tradeOffs.pro: Group Replication provides built-in Paxos membership, automatic primary election, and split-brain fencing without external Orchestrator/Zookeeper daemons.
tradeOffs.con: Every transaction pays XCom consensus RTT plus certification overhead, and large transactions (> `group_replication_transaction_size_limit`, default 150MB) fail certification.

tradeOffs.pro: Multi-primary topologies allow local writes in multiple nodes or regions without forwarding every write across a WAN.
tradeOffs.con: Auto-increment offsets (`auto_increment_increment`, `auto_increment_offset`) only prevent PK collisions; secondary unique key collisions or concurrent updates cause silent overwrites or certification aborts.

failureModes.name: Replication Lag & Stale Read-After-Write
failureModes.description: Long-running queries, single-threaded DDL (`ALTER TABLE`), or unindexed batch `DELETE` statements on the primary serialize on replicas, causing `Seconds_Behind_Source` to climb to minutes.
failureModes.mitigation: Enable `LOGICAL_CLOCK` parallel workers, set `binlog_transaction_dependency_tracking=WRITESET`, chunk large deletes to 1,000 rows, and route critical post-write reads to the primary or wait on `WAIT_FOR_EXECUTED_GTID_SET()`.

failureModes.name: Split-Brain Dual-Primary Writes
failureModes.description: Network partition triggers failover promotion of a replica while the old primary remains reachable by stale application pods, resulting in divergent GTID histories.
failureModes.mitigation: Set `super_read_only=ON` on all replicas by default, fence old primaries via ProxySQL/Orchestrator pre-failover hooks, and revoke VIPs or security-group ingress before unsetting `read_only`.

failureModes.name: Errant Transactions on Promoted Replica
failureModes.description: An operator runs a local `CREATE USER` or `DELETE` directly on a replica before promotion; its unique GTID breaks subsequent re-attachment of other replicas.
failureModes.mitigation: Enforce `super_read_only=ON` on replicas, restrict `SUPER`/`CONNECTION_ADMIN` privileges, and run `pt-table-checksum` or GTID diff checks before promotion.

failureModes.name: Purged Binlogs Before Replica Reconnect
failureModes.description: A replica goes offline for maintenance longer than `binlog_expire_logs_seconds` (default 30 days, often tuned down to 24–72h), so the primary purges needed binlogs.
failureModes.mitigation: Size `binlog_expire_logs_seconds` to at least 3x max expected maintenance/outage duration, monitor `Binlog_snapshot_position` vs. replica lag, and keep automated XtraBackup snapshots for fast re-seeding.

commonMistakes: Using `STATEMENT`-based replication with non-deterministic functions or triggers, silently corrupting replica data until checksums catch it months later.
Leaving `sync_binlog=0` or `innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit=2` on the primary, which causes binlog/InnoDB divergence or lost commits on OS crash.
Pointing application read pools directly at replicas without a health-aware proxy (ProxySQL or HAProxy) that evicts lagging replicas when `Seconds_Behind_Source > 5s`.
Running `STOP REPLICA` and skipping errors with `sql_replica_skip_counter` instead of fixing root-cause drift, compounding silent data inconsistency.
Deploying 2-node Group Replication instead of an odd quorum (3 or 5 nodes), which loses quorum whenever either node restarts.

sections.content:
## The idea

MySQL replication is an asynchronous or semi-synchronous state-machine log shipping pipeline. Every data-modifying transaction committed on the primary is recorded in the binary log (`binlog`) as row-level before/after images (`binlog_format=ROW`). Replicas connect over TCP port 3306, pull those events via an I/O receiver thread into a local `relay log`, and apply them via one or more SQL applier threads.

Topologies differ in **who can accept writes**, **how many hops events travel**, and **when the primary acknowledges a commit** to the client. Simple primary-replica topologies optimize for low write latency and read scaling; semi-synchronous topologies close the data-loss window; Group Replication replaces external failover orchestration with Paxos-based distributed consensus.

## Concrete walkthrough

Consider an order placement `INSERT INTO orders ...` on a 3-node semi-synchronous MySQL 8.0 topology (`db-primary` in AZ-1, `db-replica-1` in AZ-2, `db-replica-2` in AZ-3) with `rpl_semi_sync_source_wait_point=AFTER_SYNC` and `gtid_mode=ON`:

1. **Prepare & Binlog Write**: InnoDB prepares the transaction (`trx_id=98421`), writes undo/redo records, and appends the `GTID` event (`3e11fa47-71ca-11e1-9e33-c80aa9429562:40192`) plus `WRITE_ROWS` event to the primary's binlog, flushing with `sync_binlog=1`.
2. **Parallel Ship & Wait**: The primary's Binlog Dump thread pushes the event to `db-replica-1` and `db-replica-2`. The primary pauses *before* committing in InnoDB (`AFTER_SYNC`), holding row locks so no local session can read uncommitted state.
3. **Replica Relay Persist**: `db-replica-1`'s I/O thread writes the event to `relay-bin.000412`, flushes to disk (`sync_relay_log=1`), and sends an ACK packet back to `db-primary`.
4. **Primary Commit & Client Return**: Upon receiving 1 ACK (`rpl_semi_sync_source_wait_for_replica_count=1`), `db-primary` commits the transaction in InnoDB and returns `OK` to the application (~0.9ms total).
5. **Async Apply**: Meanwhile, `db-replica-1`'s `LOGICAL_CLOCK` worker threads apply the relay log event to its local InnoDB engine and update `gtid_executed`.

edges.description: App sends SQL COMMIT; primary writes GTID + ROW event to binlog (sync_binlog=1).

edges.title: Ship binlog event
edges.description: Primary pauses at AFTER_SYNC and streams the binlog event to connected replicas.

edges.label: Relay ACK
edges.title: Durable relay ACK
edges.description: Standby flushes event to relay log on disk and returns semi-sync ACK (~0.6ms).

edges.label: Commit OK
edges.title: InnoDB commit & return
edges.description: Primary commits in InnoDB and acknowledges client with RPO=0 guarantee.

edges.label: Async stream
edges.title: Fan-out to read pool
edges.description: Read replicas receive the same binlog stream and apply via parallel workers.

data.caption: AFTER_SYNC blocks the primary's InnoDB commit until at least one standby flushes the event to its relay log, eliminating phantom reads and lost commits on crash.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / GTIDs, parallel appliers, and topology patterns
sections.content:
## GTIDs, parallel appliers, and topology patterns

**GTIDs (`source_uuid:transaction_id`)** replace fragile `(binlog_file, offset)` coordinates. When a replica fails over to a new primary, it executes `CHANGE REPLICATION SOURCE TO SOURCE_AUTO_POSITION=1`; the new primary inspects the replica's `gtid_executed` set and streams only missing transactions.

**Parallel Replication**: Older MySQL versions applied relay logs on a single SQL thread, making a 32-core replica lag behind a 32-core primary. In MySQL 8.0, setting `binlog_transaction_dependency_tracking=WRITESET` hashes modified primary/unique keys into a dependency window so `LOGICAL_CLOCK` workers can apply non-overlapping transactions concurrently, often boosting replica apply throughput by 4x–8x.

**Common Topologies**:
- **Star (1 Primary -> N Replicas)**: Simplest; supports up to ~20–30 replicas before primary binlog dump network bandwidth saturates.
- **Tree / Cascading (Primary -> Relay -> N Replicas)**: Offloads binlog dump traffic to an intermediate `log_replica_updates=ON` relay; adds 1–5ms hop latency.
- **InnoDB Cluster (Group Replication)**: 3 or 5 nodes using XCom (Paxos) + MySQL Router; automatic quorum failover without external Orchestrator.

## Topology comparison matrix

| Topology | RPO on Primary Loss | Write Latency Impact | Max Practical Write Scale | Failover Mechanism |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Async Primary-Replica** | Seconds (unshipped binlogs lost) | None (0ms network wait) | Single primary (~20k–30k TPS) | External (Orchestrator / RDS Multi-AZ) |
| **Semi-Sync (`AFTER_SYNC`)** | 0 (for 1+ standby ACK) | +1 AZ RTT (~0.5–1.5ms) | Single primary (wait on ACK) | External + `super_read_only` fencing |
| **Cascading / Fan-out** | Seconds on leaf replicas | None on primary | Same primary; scales >50 replicas | Re-parenting leaves via GTID |
| **Group Replication (Single-Primary)** | 0 (quorum majority) | +1–2 quorum RTTs + certification | ~30%–50% lower than async | Built-in XCom Paxos election (<10s) |
| **Group Replication (Multi-Primary)** | 0 (quorum majority) | High (global certification conflicts) | Degrades sharply on hot rows | Built-in XCom; remaining nodes serve |

## Failure modes

**1. Semi-Sync Silent Downgrade to Async**: If all standbys disconnect or exceed `rpl_semi_sync_source_timeout` (default 10,000ms), MySQL automatically downgrades to asynchronous replication so writes don't hang forever. Without alerting on `Rpl_semi_sync_source_status=OFF`, teams mistakenly believe they still have RPO=0.

**2. Unbounded DDL & Large Transaction Lag**: A single `ALTER TABLE` or 5-million-row `UPDATE` writes one massive transaction to the binlog. Because a transaction cannot be applied until fully received and must run on one worker thread, replicas stall for minutes.

**3. Group Replication Flow-Control Throttling**: If one node in a 3-node InnoDB Cluster falls behind on disk IOPS, `group_replication_flow_control_mode=QUOTA` throttles writes across the *entire* cluster to prevent memory exhaustion.

## Production operations & read routing

To make replication safe for application code:

- **Read-After-Write Consistency**: Route mutations and immediate post-mutation reads (e.g., user profile updates, checkout confirmation) to the primary via ProxySQL query rules, or pass the session's `last_gtid` and block reads on `SELECT WAIT_FOR_EXECUTED_GTID_SET(?, 1)`.
- **Lag-Aware Pooling**: Configure ProxySQL `mysql_replication_hostgroups` with `max_replication_lag=5` so lagging replicas are automatically pulled from the read pool.
- **Online Schema Migrations**: Use `gh-ost` (which tails the binlog and throttles itself based on replica lag) rather than raw `ALTER TABLE` on tables over 10GB.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Enforce `gtid_mode=ON`, `enforce_gtid_consistency=ON`, and `binlog_format=ROW` across all nodes.
- [ ] Set `sync_binlog=1` and `innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit=1` on the primary for crash-safe durability.
- [ ] Enable `super_read_only=ON` on all replicas to prevent accidental errant writes.
- [ ] Configure `replica_parallel_type=LOGICAL_CLOCK`, `binlog_transaction_dependency_tracking=WRITESET`, and `replica_preserve_commit_order=ON`.
- [ ] Alert on `Seconds_Behind_Source > 5`, `Rpl_semi_sync_source_status == OFF`, and `Replica_SQL_Running == No`.
- [ ] Test automated failover quarterly in staging by killing the primary process (`kill -9`) and verifying zero split-brain.

interviewProblems.title: MySQL Replication Topologies
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on MySQL Replication Topologies. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: MySQL replication copies binary log (binlog) events from a primary server to one or more replicas to scale reads, isolate analytics, and survive node or availability-zone failures. Choosing between asynchronous, semi-synchronous, and Group Replication (Paxos-based) topologies trades write latency and operational complexity against Recovery Point Objective (RPO).

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Semi-Sync Replica (AZ-2) applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Read Replica (AZ-3).

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Read Replica (AZ-3) experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Enable `LOGICAL_CLOCK` parallel workers, set `binlog_transaction_dependency_tracking=WRITESET`, chunk large deletes to 1,000 rows, and route critical post-write reads to the primary or wait on `WAIT_FOR_EXECUTED_GTID_SET()`.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Default to GTID-based asynchronous primary-replica with semi-synchronous replication (`rpl_semi_sync_master_wait_for_slave_count=1`) when you need zero data loss on single-node failure without paying full InnoDB Group Replication consensus latency.
Avoid trap: Using `STATEMENT`-based replication with non-deterministic functions or triggers, silently corrupting replica data until checksums catch it months later.
Avoid trap: Leaving `sync_binlog=0` or `innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit=2` on the primary, which causes binlog/InnoDB divergence or lost commits on OS crash.
When to reach for it: Read-to-write ratios exceed 5:1 and SELECT traffic (dashboards, search, reporting) saturates primary buffer pool or CPU.
When to reach for it: You require zero-downtime schema changes (gh-ost or pt-online-schema-change), logical backups (mysqldump), or physical snapshots without stalling primary transactions.

putItTogether.title: Putting Mysql Replication Topologies Together
putItTogether.summary: Default to GTID-based asynchronous primary-replica with semi-synchronous replication (`rpl_semi_sync_master_wait_for_slave_count=1`) when you need zero data loss on single-node failure without paying full InnoDB Group Replication consensus latency.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Mysql Replication Topologies before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Enabling `rpl_semi_sync_source_wait_point=AFTER_SYNC` with `AFTER_SYNC` acknowledgment to a same-region standby added only 0.8ms p99 write latency while guaranteeing RPO=0 on single-AZ loss, with automatic fallback to async after a 1,000ms timeout.
